questions.q: Why isn't sp_recompile alone a lasting fix?
options: It only forces the next call to compile a fresh plan, and the same sniffing problem returns once a differently-sized provider calls it first
sp_recompile permanently disables the stored procedure
sp_recompile requires downtime to run on Azure SQL Database
sp_recompile deletes the procedure's underlying data
questions.explain: sp_recompile just resets which value gets sniffed next — it doesn't stop sniffing from happening again.

options: Forces a fresh plan to compile for this specific statement on every single execution, using that call's actual parameter value
Permanently caches one plan and never recompiles again
Deletes all statistics on the underlying tables
Only works once per day, like a scheduled job
questions.explain: OPTION (RECOMPILE) compiles a plan fresh every execution, so no plan sniffed from a different call is ever reused.

questions.q: What trade-off does this fix make?
options: More CPU cost per execution, in exchange for a plan that always fits the actual parameter passed in
No trade-off at all — it is strictly free
It trades away correctness for speed
It disables the ability to ever query dbo.Appointments again
questions.explain: Recompiling every call costs more CPU than reusing a cached plan, but it's worth it given how widely appointment counts vary per provider.

questions.q: What is the actual proof that the fix worked?
options: Timings for several providers stay consistent regardless of which order they're called in
The stored procedure's text looks cleaner after the edit
The query returns more rows than before
sp_recompile no longer exists as a valid command
questions.explain: Order-independence — no call's performance depending on which ran first — is the real proof parameter sniffing is gone, not just moved.

questions.q: Why is OPTION (RECOMPILE) not a default to reach for on every procedure?
options: A procedure called with much more uniform parameter shapes wouldn't need it, since a cached plan would already fit well
It is illegal to use on Azure SQL Database
It can only be applied to procedures with zero parameters
It always makes every procedure faster with no downside, so there's no reason not to use it everywhere
questions.explain: It's the right tool specifically for wildly varying parameter shapes causing real sniffing problems — not a universal default.
